claim: Under the climate susceptibility mechanism, the largest species possessing traits associated with diet/habitat generalism, physiological resilience to fluctuating food availability, high endurance, and rapid, efficient dispersal away from stressful conditions would persist the longest in the face of catastrophic environmental change, independent of the intensity of human predation or changing climates.

claim: The study developed the first stochastic, age-structured demographic models ever constructed for 13 extinct megafauna species in Sahul.
source: To examine the relative support of these hypotheses, we developed the first stochastic, age-structured demographic models ever constructed for 13 extinct megafauna species in Sahul broadly categorized into five functional/taxonomic groups: (i) 4 vombatiform herbivores, (ii) 5 macropodiform herbivores, (iii) 1 large, flightless bird, (iv) 2 marsupial carnivores, and (v) 1 monotreme invertivore.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the study's approach.

claim: The study also built demographic models for 8 of some of the largest, local, extant species, including representatives from each of the functional/taxonomic groups.
source: We also built demographic models for 8 of some of the largest, local, extant species, including representatives from each of the functional/taxonomic groups described above for comparison.
evidence: This is a statement about the study's approach.

claim: The null hypothesis is that extant species should demonstrate higher resilience to perturbations than the extinct species, given that they persisted through the main extinction event to the present.
source: Our null hypothesis is that these extant species should demonstrate higher resilience to perturbations than the extinct species, given that they persisted through the main extinction event to the present.
evidence: This is a statement about the study's null hypothesis.

claim: The study tested seven scenarios regarding the processes that could lead to extinction.
source: Subjecting each species' model stochastically to different types of demographic perturbations, we tested seven scenarios (described in more details in Materials and methods) regarding the processes that could lead to extinction (see also Figure 1): an allometric relationship between the time of extinction and species' body mass and/or generation length (Scenario 'LH'), reducing juvenile survival (Scenario '↓Sj') (Brook and Johnson, 2006; Munn and Dawson, 2001), reducing fertility (Scenario '↓F') (Gittleman and Thompson, 1988; Miller et al., 2016; Oftedal, 1985), reducing survival across all ages (Scenario '↓S'), individual offtake from the population via hunting (Scenario '↓ind'), increasing environmental variability generating extreme climate events causing catastrophic mortality (Scenario '↑catf'), and increasing the magnitude of environment-driven, catastrophic mortality events (Scenario '↑catM') (Reed et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a statement about the study's approach.

claim: The study hypothesizes that one, or several, of the perturbation types would provide a better match than the others between relative demographic susceptibility and the continental-scale chronology of extinctions as inferred from the fossil record.
source: We hypothesize that one, or several, of these types of perturbations would provide a better match than the others between relative demographic susceptibility and the continental-scale chronology of extinctions as inferred from the fossil record.
evidence: This is a statement about the study's hypothesis.

claim: Identifying which, if any, of the scenarios best matches the chronology would indicate higher relative support for those mechanisms being the most likely involved in driving the observed extinctions.
source: Identifying which, if any, of the scenarios best matches the chronology would therefore indicate higher relative support for those mechanisms being the most likely involved in driving the observed extinctions.
evidence: This is an inference about the implications of the study's findings.

claim: There was no indication that relatively heavier species went extinct before lighter species.

claim: There were weaker relationships between area under the quasi-extinction curve and log10 generation length for Scenarios ↓Sj, ↓ind, and ↑catf (ER <11, R2 ≤0.26).
source: The strongest relationships here were for all-ages survival-reduction (↓S) and magnitude-of-catastrophe (↑catM) scenarios (ER >490, R2 ≥0.49; Figure 4c,f), followed by weaker relationships (ER <11, R2 ≤0.26) for Scenarios ↓Sj (Figure 4a), ↓ind (Figure 4d), and ↑catf (Figure 4e), and no evidence for a relationship in Scenario ↓F (ER <1; Figure 4b).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in Figure 4a, 4d, and 4e.

claim: There was no evidence for a relationship between area under the quasi-extinction curve and log10 generation length in Scenario ↓F (ER <1).
source: The strongest relationships here were for all-ages survival-reduction (↓S) and magnitude-of-catastrophe (↑catM) scenarios (ER >490, R2 ≥0.49; Figure 4c,f), followed by weaker relationships (ER <11, R2 ≤0.26) for Scenarios ↓Sj (Figure 4a), ↓ind (Figure 4d), and ↑catf (Figure 4e), and no evidence for a relationship in Scenario ↓F (ER <1; Figure 4b).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in Figure 4b.

claim: Allometric scaling of extinction risk was apparent within most taxonomic/functional groups.
source: Allometric scaling of extinction risk was also apparent within most taxonomic/functional groups.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Diprotodon had the highest extinction risk among the extinct vombatiform herbivores in every scenario except fertility reduction.
source: For example, Diprotodon had the highest extinction risk among the extinct vombatiform herbivores in every scenario except fertility reduction (Scenario ↓F; Figures 3b and 4b).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in Figures 3b and 4b.

claim: Most species were relatively immune even to large reductions in fertility, except for Sarcophilus, Dasyurus, Vombatus, Alectura, Dromaius, and Genyornis.
source: Most species were relatively immune even to large reductions in fertility, except for Sarcophilus, Dasyurus, Vombatus, Alectura, Dromaius, and Genyornis (Figures 3b and 4b).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in Figures 3b and 4b.

claim: In the offtake sub-scenario where only juvenile individuals were removed, the results were qualitatively similar to Scenario ↓Sj where juvenile survival was progressively decreased.
source: In the offtake sub-scenario where we removed only juvenile individuals (↓indj), the results were qualitatively similar to Scenario ↓Sj where we progressively decreased juvenile survival (Appendix 7—figure 1), although the relative susceptibility for most species decreased from Scenario ↓Sj to ↓indj.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in Appendix 7—figure 1.

claim: The relative susceptibility for most species decreased from Scenario ↓Sj to ↓indj.
source: In the offtake sub-scenario where we removed only juvenile individuals (↓indj), the results were qualitatively similar to Scenario ↓Sj where we progressively decreased juvenile survival (Appendix 7—figure 1), although the relative susceptibility for most species decreased from Scenario ↓Sj to ↓indj.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in Appendix 7—figure 1.

claim: Susceptibility increased for the extinct carnivores Thylacinus and Thylacoleo from Scenario ↓Sj to ↓indj.
source: However, susceptibility increased for the extinct carnivores Thylacinus and Thylacoleo, and remained approximately the same for Dasyurus and Notamacropus (Appendix 7—figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in Appendix 7—figure 1.

claim: Susceptibility remained approximately the same for Dasyurus and Notamacropus from Scenario ↓Sj to ↓indj.
source: However, susceptibility increased for the extinct carnivores Thylacinus and Thylacoleo, and remained approximately the same for Dasyurus and Notamacropus (Appendix 7—figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in Appendix 7—figure 1.

claim: In the fertility-reduction sub-scenario where the mean number of eggs removed per female per year was progressively increased in the bird species to emulate egg harvesting by humans, there was a progressively increasing susceptibility with body mass.
source: In the fertility-reduction sub-scenario (↓Fe) where we progressively increased the mean number of eggs removed per female per year in the bird species to emulate egg harvesting by humans, there was a progressively increasing susceptibility with body mass (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in Figure 5.

claim: Genyornis was clearly the most susceptible to extinction from egg harvesting compared to the other two bird species.
source: Genyornis was clearly the most susceptible to extinction from this mechanism compared to the other two bird species (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in Figure 4 (though the text references Figure 4, it likely refers to Figure 5 based on context).

claim: When the extinction dates are viewed relative to the extinction risk calculated for each scenario, there is no indication that the most susceptible species went extinct earlier in any perturbation scenario.
source: When the extinction dates are viewed relative to the extinction risk (quasi-extinction integrals) calculated for each scenario, there is no indication that the most susceptible species went extinct earlier in any perturbation scenario (Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in Figure 6.

claim: Taking the sum of the quasi-extinction integrals across scenarios indicated that five of the eight extant species examined had extinction risks that were equivalent or higher than most of the extinct species.
source: Taking the sum of the quasi-extinction integrals across scenarios indicated that five of the eight extant species examined (Sarcophilus [extinct on mainland; extant in Tasmania], Dromaius, Alectura, Vombatus, Tachyglossus) had extinction risks that were equivalent or higher than most of the extinct species (Figure 7a).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in Figure 7a.

claim: Taking the median rank of the quasi-extinction integral across scenarios generally indicated the lowest susceptibility in the macropodiformes.
source: Taking the median rank of the quasi-extinction integral across scenarios generally indicated the lowest susceptibility in the macropodiformes (although the small, extant carnivore Dasyurus was consistently the least susceptible for all scenarios except fertility reduction; Figure 7a), followed by the carnivores (except Dasyurus), monotremes, vombatiform herbivores, and finally, large birds (Figure 7b).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in Figure 7b.

claim: The small, extant carnivore Dasyurus was consistently the least susceptible for all scenarios except fertility reduction.
source: Taking the median rank of the quasi-extinction integral across scenarios generally indicated the lowest susceptibility in the macropodiformes (although the small, extant carnivore Dasyurus was consistently the least susceptible for all scenarios except fertility reduction; Figure 7a), followed by the carnivores (except Dasyurus), monotremes, vombatiform herbivores, and finally, large birds (Figure 7b).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in Figure 7a.

claim: The carnivores had susceptibility ranks spread across most of the spectrum.
source: The carnivores had susceptibility ranks spread across most of the spectrum (Figure 7b).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in Figure 7b.

claim: Expressed as a function of log10 generation length, there was evidence for a moderate relationship across all species (ER = 12.07, R2 = 0.27).
source: Expressed as a function of log10 generation length, there was evidence for a moderate relationship across all species (ER = 12.07, R2 = 0.27; Figure 7c), but removing the outlier species Sarcophilus and Dromaius resulted in a much stronger relationship (ER = 3.61 × 105, R2 = 0.76; Figure 7c).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in Figure 7c.

claim: Removing the outlier species Sarcophilus and Dromaius resulted in a much stronger relationship between median susceptibility rank and log10 generation length (ER = 3.61 × 105, R2 = 0.76).
source: Expressed as a function of log10 generation length, there was evidence for a moderate relationship across all species (ER = 12.07, R2 = 0.27; Figure 7c), but removing the outlier species Sarcophilus and Dromaius resulted in a much stronger relationship (ER = 3.61 × 105, R2 = 0.76; Figure 7c).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in Figure 7c.

claim: Susceptibility tended to increase with body mass within a group, except for carnivores and monotremes.
source: Susceptibility also tended to increase with body mass within a group, except for carnivores (Sarcophilus being the anomaly) and monotremes (Figure 7c).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in Figure 7c.

claim: There was no indication of a pattern when extinction date is plotted against median susceptibility rank.
source: There was no indication of a pattern when extinction date is plotted against median susceptibility rank (Figure 7d).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in Figure 7d.

claim: The megafauna species of Sahul demonstrate demographic susceptibility to extinction largely following expectations derived from threat risk in modern species — species with slower life histories have higher demographic risk to extinction on average.
source: The megafauna species of Sahul demonstrate demographic susceptibility to extinction largely following expectations derived from threat risk in modern species — species with slower life histories have higher demographic risk to extinction on average (Cardillo et al., 2005; Liow et al., 2008; Purvis et al., 2000; Tomiya, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cardillo et al., 2005; Liow et al., 2008; Purvis et al., 2000; Tomiya, 2013.

claim: The models show a convincing relationship between a taxon's overall relative demographic susceptibility to extinction and its generation length.
source: Indeed, our models show a convincing relationship between a taxon's overall relative demographic susceptibility to extinction and its generation length.
evidence: This claim is supported by the results of the stochastic demographic models presented in the manuscript.

claim: Demography clearly must have played a role in the extinction of Sahul's megafauna given that mainly the largest species succumbed.
source: While demography clearly must have played a role in the extinction of Sahul's megafauna given that mainly the largest species succumbed (Lyons et al., 2016), our stochastic models revealed no clear relationship between relative demographic susceptibility and the order in which the taxa we considered went extinct (even after considering alternative approaches to calculate the window of extinction — Appendix 8—figure 1–3).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lyons et al., 2016.

claim: The stochastic models revealed no clear relationship between relative demographic susceptibility and the order in which the taxa went extinct.
source: While demography clearly must have played a role in the extinction of Sahul's megafauna given that mainly the largest species succumbed (Lyons et al., 2016), our stochastic models revealed no clear relationship between relative demographic susceptibility and the order in which the taxa we considered went extinct (even after considering alternative approaches to calculate the window of extinction — Appendix 8—figure 1–3).
evidence: This claim is supported by the results of the stochastic demographic models presented in the manuscript.

claim: The study did not find that the most demographically susceptible species went extinct before more resilient species.
source: In particular, we did not find that the most demographically susceptible species went extinct before more resilient species.
evidence: This claim is supported by the results of the stochastic demographic models presented in the manuscript.

claim: The actual extinction chronology must have been an emergent property of many interacting demographic rates, temporal and spatial variation in population abundance, particular environmental contexts, community interactions, and likely other traits.
source: We can only conclude that the actual extinction chronology must have instead been an emergent property of many interacting demographic rates, temporal and spatial variation in population abundance, particular environmental contexts, community interactions, and likely other traits (Sodhi et al., 2009).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the lack of relationship between demographic susceptibility and extinction chronology, supported by a citation to Sodhi et al., 2009.

claim: As different perturbations compromise different aspects of a species' life history, its relative susceptibility to extinction compared to other species in its community varies in often unpredictable ways.
source: As different perturbations compromise different aspects of a species' life history, its relative susceptibility to extinction compared to other species in its community varies in often unpredictable ways.
evidence: This is an inference based on the results of the stochastic demographic models.

claim: The study rejects the hypothesis that the continent-wide extinction chronology is explained by species' relative demographic susceptibility and non-selective hunting by humans.
source: We can therefore reject the hypothesis that the continent-wide extinction chronology is explained by species' relative demographic susceptibility and non-selective hunting by humans.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the lack of relationship between demographic susceptibility and extinction chronology.

claim: If demographic susceptibility coupled with non-selective hunting were the primary causes of these extinctions, we would expect a relationship between vulnerability and extinction date whereby the more vulnerable species went extinct earlier — but no such relationship was found.
source: If demographic susceptibility coupled with non-selective hunting were the primary causes of these extinctions, we would expect a relationship between vulnerability and extinction date whereby the more vulnerable species went extinct earlier — but we found no such relationship (Figure 7d).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the lack of relationship between demographic susceptibility and extinction chronology, supported by data in Figure 7d.

claim: The comparison of susceptibility under increasing intensities of egg harvesting revealed the highest demographic risk from this type of activity for the extinct Genyornis compared to the extant Dromaius and Alectura birds.
source: However, the comparison of susceptibility under increasing intensities of egg harvesting revealed the highest demographic risk from this type of activity for the extinct Genyornis compared to the extant Dromaius and Alectura birds, supporting the notion that egg harvesting (and not hunting of adults) might have been at least partially responsible for the demise of Genyornis (Miller et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by the results of the stochastic demographic models presented in the manuscript.

claim: Egg harvesting (and not hunting of adults) might have been at least partially responsible for the demise of Genyornis.
source: However, the comparison of susceptibility under increasing intensities of egg harvesting revealed the highest demographic risk from this type of activity for the extinct Genyornis compared to the extant Dromaius and Alectura birds, supporting the notion that egg harvesting (and not hunting of adults) might have been at least partially responsible for the demise of Genyornis (Miller et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the results of the stochastic demographic models, supported by a citation to Miller et al., 2016.

claim: The study rejects the hypothesis that the largest, and therefore the most physiologically buffered and mobile species, were the most resilient given the lack of relationship with the inferred extinction chronology.
source: We can also reject the hypothesis that the largest, and therefore the most physiologically buffered and mobile species, were the most resilient given the lack of relationship with the inferred extinction chronology (Figures 2 and 7d).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the lack of relationship between body mass and extinction chronology, supported by data in Figures 2 and 7d.

claim: The species with the highest sensitivities to reductions arising from the various perturbation scenarios did not succumb earlier.
source: Neither did the species with the highest sensitivities to reductions arising from the various perturbation scenarios succumb earlier (Figures 5 and 6d).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in Figures 5 and 6d.

claim: The lack of relationship to the chronology, combined with the result that many of the extant species had some of the highest extinction susceptibilities, suggest that no obvious demographic properties can explain the taxon-specific timing within the Sahul extinction event of the Late Pleistocene.
source: This lack of relationship to the chronology, combined with the result that many of the extant species had some of the highest extinction susceptibilities, suggest that no obvious demographic properties can explain the taxon-specific timing within the Sahul extinction event of the Late Pleistocene.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the results of the stochastic demographic models.

claim: The chronology might reflect either a random set of circumstances — that species succumbed to circumstantial combinations of stressors depending on the local perturbations experienced by particular populations — or even that the chronology is still insufficiently resolved.
source: This opens the possibility that the chronology instead reflects either a random set of circumstances — that species succumbed to circumstantial combinations of stressors depending on the local perturbations experienced by particular populations (Saltré et al., 2019) — or even that the chronology is still insufficiently resolved.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the inference that demographic susceptibility alone does not explain the extinction chronology, supported by a citation to Saltré et al., 2019.

claim: The conclusion that the chronology might reflect random circumstances does not accord well with the notion that Late Pleistocene megafauna extinctions were non-random and occurred at a much higher pace than background extinction rates.
source: However, this conclusion does not accord well with the notion that Late Pleistocene megafauna extinctions were non-random and occurred at a much higher pace than background extinction rates (Johnson, 2006; Koch and Barnosky, 2006).
evidence: This is an inference about the implications of the study's findings, supported by citations to Johnson, 2006 and Koch and Barnosky, 2006.

claim: In the case of human hunting, preferences for selecting or avoiding particular species, such as targeting larger species for more efficient returns, could have overridden or interacted with intrinsic demographic susceptibility.
source: Another possibility is that in the case of human hunting, preferences for selecting or avoiding particular species, such as targeting larger species for more efficient returns (Broughton et al., 2011), could have overridden or interacted with intrinsic demographic susceptibility.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the inference that demographic susceptibility alone does not explain the extinction chronology, supported by a citation to Broughton et al., 2011.

claim: Lyons et al., 2016 concluded that either large-bodied mammals were selectively targeted by humans during the Late Quaternary, or that these species were relatively more vulnerable to human hunting than smaller-bodied species, or both.
source: Indeed, Lyons et al., 2016 concluded that either large-bodied mammals were selectively targeted by humans during the Late Quaternary, or that these species were relatively more vulnerable to human hunting than smaller-bodied species, or both.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lyons et al., 2016.

claim: Specific behavioural adaptations could potentially have rendered demographically high-risk species in fact less vulnerable to human hunting, such as the behavior of Vombatus to dig and defend burrows that were difficult to access by humans compared to larger burrowing or non-burrowing vombatiformes.
source: In addition, specific behavioural adaptations could potentially have rendered demographically high-risk species in fact less vulnerable to human hunting, such as the behavior of Vombatus to dig and defend burrows that were difficult to access by humans (Garvey et al., 2016) compared to larger burrowing or non-burrowing vombatiformes.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the inference that demographic susceptibility alone does not explain the extinction chronology, supported by a citation to Garvey et al., 2016.

claim: In the case of the macropodiformes, interspecific variation in the type of locomotion could have contributed more to their relative susceptibility to human hunters.
source: In the case of the macropodiformes, interspecific variation in the type of locomotion — a trait not captured by our demographic models — could have contributed more to their relative susceptibility to human hunters.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the inference that demographic susceptibility alone does not explain the extinction chronology.

claim: The ability to hop at high velocities as in Osphranter rufus could have given it an escape advantage over the relatively slower sthenurine macropodiformes that likely employed more bipedal striding than hopping.
source: For example, the ability to hop at high velocities as in Osphranter rufus could have given it an escape advantage over the relatively slower sthenurine macropodiformes that likely employed more bipedal striding than hopping (Janis et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the inference that demographic susceptibility alone does not explain the extinction chronology, supported by a citation to Janis et al., 2020.

claim: Similar hypotheses regarding risk-persistence mismatches in multispecies simulations have been proposed for the Late Pleistocene megafauna extinction event in North America.
source: Similar hypotheses regarding risk-persistence mismatches in multispecies simulations have been proposed for the Late Pleistocene megafauna extinction event in North America (Alroy, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Alroy, 2001.

claim: Marsupials are widely included in studies estimating the types of mammalian demographic relationships used in this study.
source: Although marsupials are widely included in studies estimating the types of mammalian demographic relationships like those we used here (de Magalhães et al., 2007; Healy et al., 2014; McCarthy et al., 2008), more explicit consideration of their reproductive differences compared to placentals might further improve the resolution of future models.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to de Magalhães et al., 2007; Healy et al., 2014; McCarthy et al., 2008.

claim: More explicit consideration of marsupials' reproductive differences compared to placentals might further improve the resolution of future models.
source: Although marsupials are widely included in studies estimating the types of mammalian demographic relationships like those we used here (de Magalhães et al., 2007; Healy et al., 2014; McCarthy et al., 2008), more explicit consideration of their reproductive differences compared to placentals might further improve the resolution of future models.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential improvements to future models.

claim: Marsupials are born at the extreme altricial stage and complete most of their development ex utero through lactation.
source: In particular, marsupials are born at the extreme altricial stage and complete most of their development ex utero through lactation (Tyndale-Biscoe, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Tyndale-Biscoe, 2005.

claim: The unusually long period of marsupial lactation can reduce the cost of raising offspring per unit time.
source: This might change the way the cost of reproduction is borne, because the unusually long period of marsupial lactation can reduce the cost of raising offspring per unit time (Cork and Dove, 1989; Weisbecker and Goswami, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cork and Dove, 1989 and Weisbecker and Goswami, 2010.

claim: There is an increasing number of small marsupial and placental mammals known to have gone extinct during the Pleistocene in Sahul.
source: There is also an increasing number of small marsupial and placental mammals known to have gone extinct during the Pleistocene in Sahul (e.g. Cramb et al., 2009; Cramb et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cramb et al., 2009 and Cramb et al., 2018.

claim: The inclusion of smaller species in future demographic susceptibility/chronology of extinction analyses will likely be insightful, but estimates of extinction dates are not yet available for these animals.
source: The inclusion of these smaller species in future demographic susceptibility/chronology of extinction analyses will likely be insightful, but unfortunately estimates of extinction dates — which require at least 8–10 reliability dated specimens (Bradshaw et al., 2012; Saltré et al., 2015) — are not yet available for these animals.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential future research, supported by citations to Bradshaw et al., 2012 and Saltré et al., 2015.

claim: The models, although age-structured, stochastic, and incorporating compensatory density feedback, are still simplified expressions of a species' particular ecological and environmental contexts.
source: Our models, although age-structured, stochastic, and incorporating compensatory density feedback, are still simplified expressions of a species' particular ecological and environmental contexts.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the limitations of the study's models.

claim: The models are aspatial, yet spatial processes are known to be correlated with local extinctions across the landscape.
source: As stated, our models are aspatial, yet we know that spatial processes are correlated with local extinctions across the landscape (Saltré et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the limitations of the study's models, supported by a citation to Saltré et al., 2019.

claim: Large proboscideans like mammoths managed to persist well into the Holocene on island refugia despite having a high intrinsic extinction risk.
source: For example, large proboscideans like mammoths managed to persist well into the Holocene on island refugia despite having a high intrinsic extinction risk (Nogués-Bravo et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Nogués-Bravo et al., 2008.

claim: It is plausible that more localized measures of extinction risk, timing, and particular climate and habitat contexts could reveal subtler demographic processes at work.
source: It is therefore plausible that more localized measures of extinction risk, timing, and particular climate and habitat contexts (see Appendix 9 for an examination of demographic susceptibility relative to hindcasted climate trends) could reveal subtler demographic processes at work (Chase et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential future research, supported by a citation to Chase et al., 2020.

claim: Sahul's fossil record is still generally too sparse at a regional level to test localized measures of extinction risk properly.
source: However, Sahul's fossil record is still generally too sparse at a regional level to test this properly (Peters et al., 2019; Rodríguez-Rey et al., 2016), nor do we have data indicating how spatial variation might have altered local expressions of demographic rates in long-extinct species.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Peters et al., 2019 and Rodríguez-Rey et al., 2016.

claim: The models ignore biotic dependencies such as predator-prey, plant-herbivore, and competition relationships that could have modified relative susceptibility in different ways depending on the community in question.
source: Our models also ignore biotic dependencies such as predator-prey, plant-herbivore, and competition relationships that could have modified relative susceptibility in different ways depending on the community in question (Brook and Bowman, 2004; Choquenot and Bowman, 1998).
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the limitations of the study's models, supported by citations to Brook and Bowman, 2004 and Choquenot and Bowman, 1998.

claim: Trophic community networks constructed for south-eastern Sahul show that bottom-up processes most strongly affect lower trophic levels, with their influence diminishing at higher trophic levels.
source: Trophic community networks constructed for south-eastern Sahul show that bottom-up processes most strongly affect lower trophic levels, with their influence diminishing at higher trophic levels, although extinct carnivores were more vulnerable to coextinction than extant carnivores (Llewelyn et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Llewelyn et al., 2020.

claim: Extinct carnivores were more vulnerable to coextinction than extant carnivores.
source: Trophic community networks constructed for south-eastern Sahul show that bottom-up processes most strongly affect lower trophic levels, with their influence diminishing at higher trophic levels, although extinct carnivores were more vulnerable to coextinction than extant carnivores (Llewelyn et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Llewelyn et al., 2020.

claim: The particulars of the Genyornis extinction are still debatable given the possibility that the egg shells used to date the species are potentially confounded with an extinct Progura megapode.
source: The particulars of the Genyornis extinction are also still debatable given the possibility that the egg shells used to date the species (Miller et al., 2005) are potentially confounded with an extinct Progura megapode (Grellet-Tinner et al., 2016; Shute et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Miller et al., 2005; Grellet-Tinner et al., 2016; Shute et al., 2017.

claim: Removing 'Genyornis' from the extinction chronology makes no difference to the overall conclusions.
source: However, removing 'Genyornis' from the extinction chronology makes no difference to our overall conclusions, but it is problematic for comparing relative extinction risk between the extinct Genyornis and the extant Dromaius and Alectura.
evidence: This is an inference based on the results of the stochastic demographic models.

claim: By including an extant megapode (Alectura) in the model simulations, the study determined that this much smaller (2.2 kg) and faster-reproducing species had a much lower extinction susceptibility than both Genyornis and Dromaius.
source: In fact, by including an extant megapode (Alectura) in our model simulations, we determined that this much smaller (2.2 kg) and faster-reproducing species had a much lower extinction susceptibility than both Genyornis and Dromaius.
evidence: This claim is supported by the results of the stochastic demographic models presented in the manuscript.

claim: The finding of no clear patterns among the extinct megafauna of Sahul to explain their relative extinction chronology supports the notion that, at least for mammals, risk can be high across all body masses depending on a species' particular ecology.
source: That we found no clear patterns among the extinct megafauna of Sahul to explain their relative extinction chronology supports the notion that, at least for mammals, risk can be high across all body masses depending on a species' particular ecology (Davidson et al., 2009), even if relative extinction risk appears to follow allometric expectations (Brook and Bowman, 2005; Cardillo et al., 2005; Liow et al., 2008; Purvis et al., 2000; Tomiya, 2013) as we demonstrated clearly here (Figures 3, 5 and 7).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the results of the stochastic demographic models, supported by citations to Davidson et al., 2009; Brook and Bowman, 2005; Cardillo et al., 2005; Liow et al., 2008; Purvis et al., 2000; Tomiya, 2013.

claim: By definition, the megafauna were generally large (>45 kg) species.
source: By definition, the megafauna were generally large (>45 kg) species, yet neither their body mass or their correspondingly higher relative demographic susceptibility explains the extinction chronology in Sahul.
evidence: This is a statement about the definition of megafauna.

claim: Neither the body mass nor the correspondingly higher relative demographic susceptibility of megafauna explains the extinction chronology in Sahul.
source: By definition, the megafauna were generally large (>45 kg) species, yet neither their body mass or their correspondingly higher relative demographic susceptibility explains the extinction chronology in Sahul.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the results of the stochastic demographic models.

claim: The study's approach provides a template for assessing relative demographic susceptibility to extinction for other Sahul species not considered in this study, and for those in other continents.
source: Our approach also provides a template for assessing relative demographic susceptibility to extinction for other Sahul species that we did not consider here, and for those in other continents, that could reveal previously underappreciated dynamics and drivers.
evidence: This is a statement about the potential applications of the study's approach.

claim: More spatially and community-dependent models are still needed to provide a more complete picture of the dynamics of Late Pleistocene megafauna extinctions.
source: Nonetheless, more spatially and community-dependent models are still needed to provide a more complete picture of the dynamics of Late Pleistocene megafauna extinctions.
evidence: This is a statement about the need for future research.

claim: The study chose enough extinct and extant species from the Sahul fossil record to represent a diversity of clades that were particularly affected during the main extinction event (estimated between 60 and 40 ka).
source: Our first step was to choose enough extinct and extant species from the Sahul fossil record (Peters et al., 2019; Rodríguez-Rey et al., 2016) to represent a diversity of clades that were particularly affected during the main extinction event (estimated between 60 and 40 ka, where one ka = 1000 years ago) (Saltré et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement about the study's methodology, supported by citations to Peters et al., 2019; Rodríguez-Rey et al., 2016; Saltré et al., 2016.

claim: The main extinction event in Sahul is estimated to have occurred between 60 and 40 ka.
source: Our first step was to choose enough extinct and extant species from the Sahul fossil record (Peters et al., 2019; Rodríguez-Rey et al., 2016) to represent a diversity of clades that were particularly affected during the main extinction event (estimated between 60 and 40 ka, where one ka = 1000 years ago) (Saltré et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Saltré et al., 2016.

claim: The study aimed to include at least one extant species within each functional/taxonomic group to compare extant with extinct species' susceptibility.
source: We also aimed to include at least one extant species within each functional/taxonomic group to compare extant with extinct species' susceptibility.
evidence: This is a statement about the study's methodology.

claim: The study settled on a total of 21 species (13 extinct; 8 extant) from five different functional/taxonomic groups.
source: We settled on a total of 21 species (13 extinct; 8 extant) from five different functional/taxonomic groups: (i) 5 vombatiform herbivores, (ii) 7 macropodiform herbivores, (iii) 3 large birds, (iv) 4 carnivores, and (v) 2 monotreme invertivores.
evidence: This is a statement about the study's methodology.

claim: To build age-structured population models for extinct taxa, the study relied on different allometric, phylogenetic, and measured relationships to predict the plausible range of component demographic rates.
source: To build age-structured population models for extinct taxa, we relied on different allometric, phylogenetic, and measured relationships to predict the plausible range of component demographic rates.
